  annotation files which label objects within images.  However, object annotations
  are costly and time-consuming to create, as they require a significant amount
  of expert time for proper labeling.  It's not uncommon for a single annotation
  dataset to require the effort of multiple experts over an extended period.
  Object annotation is a labor-intensive process that can limit the availability
  of high-quality datasets and hinder the widespread use of deep learning-based
  object detection techniques within real-world applications.
  Transfer learning through object annotation is a promising approach to speed up
  the labeling process.  In this approach, a small set of annotations is used
  to label objects within a limited set of images, with the goal that these
  annotations can be transferred to other previously unannotated images.
  YOLOv3 is a popular and lightweight object detection algorithm known for its
  simple and efficient approach to object detection within real-time frameworks.
  However, the limited customization options of the YOLOv3 algorithm restrict
  its ability to effectively transfer learned object annotations.
  A new algorithm called AnnoTransfer YOLOv3 addresses this limitation by
  introducing a set of training techniques that enable the successful transfer of
  object annotations.  This is achieved by modifying the YOLOv3 algorithm to
  include a region of interest module that detects and extracts regions of
  interest within images, followed by a classification module that classifies
  objects within these regions, with the assistance of a massive pre-trained
  feature extraction database.
  Evaluations of the AnnoTransfer YOLOv3 algorithm on real-world images reveal
  a significant decrease in the number of images that require manual object
  annotations.  For example, a dataset of 1000 images may only require 100
  manually annotated objects to achieve comparable results.  The AnnoTransfer
  YOLOv3 algorithm demonstrates a notable increase in the accuracy of transferred
  object annotations when compared to the current state-of-the-art approaches.
  Furthermore, the AnnoTransfer YOLOv3 algorithm exhibits a notable improvement
  in speed and efficiency when compared to the current state-of-the-art
  object detection frameworks.  The AnnoTransfer YOLOv3 algorithm achieves an
  object detection accuracy of 82.5\% on the VOC 2007 dataset with a small
  set of manually annotated objects, placing it among the top performing

Moreover, our research also introduces a new family of branching random walks with migration that serve as polynomial generalizations of the classical binary tree model. This theorem demonstrates that solutions with an initial condition that belongs to a certain interpolation space will have a regular boundary for a certain period of time. In particular, this shows that solutions with initial conditions from $L^p$ spaces will have a regular boundary for a time period that scales as $t^{(d-\min(p,2))/2}$. This means that a solution with an initial condition from an $L^p$ space will have a smooth boundary for almost all positive times. This improves an earlier result from the literature, which stated that the time during which the solution has a regular boundary is at least $t^{(d-\min(p,2))/2}$, but did not account for the cases when $p>4$ or $d>4$.   Users' preference patterns, particularly in community-based platforms, form 
  through repeated interactions and shape their future preferences.
  These unexplored preferences can be represented as similarity among users and 
  entities and are particularly important for recommending content in forums and 
  social networks.
  To address this issue, an unsupervised method is presented that extracts and 
  models these unexplored preferences in multi-entity graphs.
  The proposed approach, called Unexplored Preference Graph Attention Network (UP-GAN),
  leverages the structure of graphs to learn attention-based weights that determine 
  the importance of explicit and unexplored edges for recommendation purposes.
  UP-GAN extracts novel relationships by combining the unexplored similarities among 
  users and entities and fuses them with the existing edges in the graph.
  A strategy is designed to generate negative samples that mimic the behavior of 
  unexplored edges for the purpose of training an robust recommender system.
  Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that UP-GAN performs 
  comparably to or exceeds current state-of-the-art methods in recommendation 
  accuracy tasks, proving the effectiveness of the approach.  An analysis of the 
  importance of unexplored edges within the graphs is also conducted to provide 
  insights into when and why these unexplored preferences are crucial for recommending 
  content.  Furthermore, an evaluation of UP-GAN is performed in an unsupervised 
  setting where the knowledge extraction process is assessed independently, and the 
  obtained knowledge is utilized in various graph-based applications.  The findings 
  indicate that an initial exploration of the graph is valuable for a comprehensive 
  understanding of the underlying preferences, and this knowledge can be utilized for 
  recommending content.  To facilitate further research, the datasets, code, and 
  instructions for reproducing the experiments are made available.  An evaluation

  systems is proposed and established through an agreement among multiple experts in

  various graph-based recommender system datasets.  An open-source implementation 
  of UP-GAN in Python, along with the reproducible experiment setup, is made

This paper introduces a streaming algorithm that produces $\epsilon$-Nash equilibria in games played over time, resulting in a socially optimal outcome with a $\phi$-factor increase in costs, bounded by a polynomial of the number of players, time steps, and relevant parameters. Having access to comprehensive and detailed maps of every environment would make this possible, but it's impractical due to the extensive time and resources required for accurate lidar mapping.  To address this issue, a method is proposed for rapidly gathering high-quality spatial maps in unexplored territories using a mobility network.  An important challenge in this process is creating a unified map that links multiple separate scans, even when mobility paths are known.  This problem is further complicated by the need for maps to be compact and free from holes to ensure the robots can move freely and navigate easily.  To overcome these obstacles, a new framework is presented that integrates a matching algorithm with a mobility graph to find the optimal way to combine lidar scans.  The proposed method is tested on a series of mobility trails with different shapes to evaluate its versatility, and a indoor experiment is also conducted to demonstrate its applicability in real-world scenarios.  Specifically, a mobility trail with a known path consisting of 14 points was tested, and the results showed that this method is capable of creating compact maps from a wide range of experiences with varying shapes, as seen in \ref{fig:traj14}.  A more complex indoor trail with a unknown path was also successfully mapped, and the introduced holes in the map are shown in \ref{fig:indoor_map_holes}.  A quantitative evaluation of the proposed method is also presented in \ref{quantitative_evaluation}.  To facilitate widespread use, the proposed algorithm's code is made publicly available at: https://github.com/shaymath12/lidar_map_merge. This code and dataset can serve as a foundation for more advanced spatial mapping techniques and provide valuable resources for testing and evaluating such methods.   from recent experiments, it's suggested that the actual distribution of event 
  spacings deviates significantly from this expected pattern, exhibiting a 
  phenomenon known as anti-Poissonality. To better grasp the mechanisms driving 
  material deformation, researchers propose utilizing a mathematical model that 
  analyzes the statistics of event spacings and identifies anti-Poissonality in 
  experiments using nanosecond-scale resolution. For titanium alloy GRAIN, 
  researchers were able to demonstrate a connection between the deviation from 
  Poissonality and the spatial and temporal arrangements of dislocations. 
  Specifically, it's found that shear bands that form in titanium alloy GRAIN, 
  which are characterized by high displacement rates and dense dislocation 
  arrangements, are responsible for the deviation from Poissonality, and this 
  connection holds true even at scales as small as 20 nanometers. 
  Consequently, researchers believe that more thoroughly studying anti-Poissonality 
  in material deformation could lead to a deeper understanding of dislocation 
  dynamics and their role in shaping the mechanical properties of materials. 
  Furthermore, researchers also propose that analyzing the statistics of event 
  spacings could be an invaluable tool for developing more accurate predictive 
  models for material deformation. 
  The proposed research approach, which utilizes a previously established 
  experimental setup, involves conducting in-situ compression experiments on 
  titanium alloy GRAIN during plastic deformation. However, unlike previous 
  experiments, the proposed setup would allow researchers to examine the statistics 
  of event spacings at multiple strain rates. Consequently, researchers believe 
  that conducting such experiments could lead to findings that clarify the mechanical 
  signals associated with dislocation dynamics and provide quantitative insights 
  into the statistics of event spacings in materials exhibiting anti-Poissonality. 
  Furthermore, researchers also propose to examine the connection between the observed 
  anti-Poissonality and the mechanical properties of materials by analyzing the statistics 
  of event spacings at different scales, in addition to investigating the effects 
  of varying dislocation densities, shear band formation, and grain boundary activity 
  on the statistics of event spacings.

  where no further interactions with the environment are allowed after data collection.
  This setting is crucial for applying reinforcement learning in safety-critical domains, such
  as medical treatment and financial management, where trial and error through actual
  experiments is unacceptable.
  Unfortunately, the intransparency of the underlying value function and policy from
  the collected dataset hinders offline reinforcement learning, making it difficult to
  determine an optimal action sequence and complicating the process of obtaining
  statistical insights.
  To overcome these challenges, a new theoretical framework for offline reinforcement
  learning is presented, which for the first time provides rigorous conditions to ensure
  the convergence of policy optimization in an offline setting.
  Specifically, the requirements of the proposed framework include sufficient smoothness
  of the value function, the existence of a minimum policy, and the collection of
  robust and diverse training data.
  To achieve the latter, the paper introduces an unsupervised data quality assessment
  method that filters the most representative and high-quality samples from the
  collected dataset without relying on knowledge of the environment or the underlying
  value function and policy.
  Furthermore, the paper explores the application of its framework to the
  optimization of a linear value function and policy in multi-arm bandits, which is
  useful for modeling medical treatment scenarios.

  Natural Policy Gradient.

  effectiveness of the proposed framework in achieving policy optimization in an

  Although valuable, cod summarization's simplicity makes it 
  difficult to evaluate, as the accuracy of its associated metrics 
  is questioned due to the limited scope and subjectivity of 
  code summaries. In response to these challenges, a cod summarization 
  evaluation method is proposed, based on the assumption that 
  good cod summarization should result in more beneficial outcomes 
  for developers when compared to less accurate cod summarization. 
  To put this approach to the test, a cod summarization evaluation 
  framework was created and used in a study to assess the performance 
  of five baselines and three state-of-the-art models on cod summarization 
  tasks, using relevant metrics alongside the proposed evaluation method. 
  The results showed that the proposed evaluation method effectively 
  differentiates between cod summarization models of higher and lower 
  quality, as determined by its association with more favorable 
  outcomes for developers in real-world scenarios. 
  Furthermore, the proposed evaluation framework was found to provide 
  valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of cod summarization 
  models, as well as valuable predictions for developers in need of 
  code information. In particular, the proposed evaluation method 
  successfully identified code segments that the associated cod summarization 
  models incorrectly associated with relevant comments, as well as 
  code segments that the associated cod summarization models failed 
  to correctly identify.

lattice gauge theories can be extremely computationally costly due to the large number of degrees of freedom involved in field interactions, a problem that becomes especially acute when trying to perform Monte Carlo simulations of these theories. A potential solution involves using gauge invariant few-body physics tools, which could provide a significant reduction in computational demands while still capturing essential aspects of field interactions and correlations. This paper discusses the development of a lattice gauge theory approach that models electron-electron interactions in a finite system by describing the behavior of a small group of lattice sites rather than an infinite lattice, and demonstrates through calculations on small lattice configurations that this method accurately reproduces the results of the full electron-electron interaction calculation. Furthermore, we show that this model can be extended to describe the behavior of larger groups of lattice sites and derive an exact relation between the homologous Wess-Zumino-Witten field theory and the lattice gauge theory of electron-electron interactions. Additionally, we provide a numerical illustration of our model's capabilities by calculating the pair correlation function in a lattice gauge theory of electron-electron interactions. Moreover, we show that this model also correctly reproduces the results of the full electron-electron interaction calculation when considering the effects of long-range interactions. A key feature of this model is that it can be easily implemented on a minimal lattice, a feature that could be particularly useful for an experimental realization of a lattice gauge theory. A major breakthrough in this research is the derivation of an exact relation between the homologous Wess-Zumino-Witten field theory and the lattice gauge theory of electron-electron interactions, an achievement that also reveals the underlying field theory describing small groups of lattice sites as a Wess-Zumino-Witten field theory.   We derive the subdifferential formulas for the composite function $f\circ g$ and the potential $f^{**}$ of a proper convex function $f$, assuming $f$ and $g$ have certain growth properties.
  Specifically, we establish that the subdifferential of $f\circ g$ at a point $x$ equals the image of the subdifferential of $f$ at $f(x)$ under the adjoint map of the derivative of $g$ at $x$.
  We also obtain an equivalent formulation for the subdifferential of $f^{**}$, which enables us to pose and solve specific optimization problems.
  We then apply our results to convex optimization problems involving functions of quadratic mean, for which we derive the optimal solutions and provide an analysis of the problem's properties.
  We also investigate the connection between these problems and those involving $f$-divergence, establishing that many optimization problems of this type are equivalent to those of quadratic mean, thus yielding a broader class of problems solvable via our established convex optimization techniques. 
  We further examine the fundamental case of Kullback-Leibler divergence and demonstrate that minimizing its relative entropy is tantamount to maximizing the logarithmic mean of the two pertinent probability measures. 
  We also derive the optimal solutions to these problems in the form of means for a broad category of convex functions, including specifically $f$-divergences defined by non-decreasing convex functions with respect to subadditivity. 
  We also establish that the optimal solutions to these problems are closed subspaces if the underlying measures are equal and that the conditional expectation serves as the optimal solution multiplier. 
  We also determine the optimal solutions to problems of quadratic mean for specific convex functions, establishing that they are means if and only if the functions satisfy submultiplicative properties. 
  We also derive the formula for the subdifferential of the log-sum-exp function, which enables us to pose and solve various optimization problems involving relative entropy. 
  We also establish that the optimization problems of quadratic mean are equivalent to those of $f$-divergence when considering the convex functions $f(s) = s\log s$ and $f(s) = (e^s-1)/e$, respectively. 
  We also provide an in-depth analysis of the properties of means, establishing that they are closed convex sets defined by the constraints of quadratic mean

Our  current understanding of the IMF's dependence on environment lacks observational  evidence to support top-heavy IMFs in typical star-forming galaxies, except  for the mentioned cases of dwarf galaxies.  To investigate the relationship  between galaxy environment and IMF, we conducted a statistical analysis of  1,441 resolved star clusters observed in 11 local and distant galaxies using  6 different surveys.  We used three standard IMF prescriptions and a fourth  that fits a normal distribution to analyze the stellar masses of individual  cluster members.  Our results show that while the IMF may vary among clusters  forming in different galaxies, the most significant trend is a negative  correlation with galactic mass, specifically in galaxies with stellar masses  10^8-10^11 solar masses.  This relationship is consistent with observations  of the gas reservoirs of star clusters and can be explained by their mass-dependent  supernova feedback.  However, we found no evidence supporting the hypothesis  that the IMF is systematically different in dwarf galaxies compared to massive  galaxies, thus challenging the notion of mass-dependent IMFs.  Instead, we  propose that the previously observed correlation might be an indirect effect of  varying mass clusters forming in different galaxies, supported by our findings  from the most extensive cluster databases used to date.  Our research also  examined the relationship between cluster stellar mass and galactic metallicity,  finding a positive correlation that is likely caused by metal-rich clusters forming  in more massive galaxies.  However, when controlling for galaxy mass, we found  no distinction in the behavior of low- and high-mass clusters with respect to  galactic metallicity.  Our findings have significant implications for the theoretical  models of galaxy and star cluster formation and suggest that the relationship  between galaxy environment and IMF needs to be further explored using a broader  range of galaxy masses and metallicities.   energetic interactions and can capture particles traveling at up to 325 
  degrees from the beam pipe. The silicon pixel detector operates at a 
  speed of 40 MHz and can identify particles traveling at speeds of up to 
  99.7% the speed of light. The detector's low power design and robust

  LHC collisions at energies as high as 13 TeV.  The detector's

  evolution of galaxies within the Milky Way's halo through the ages, with a 
  focus on the development of bulges. To that end, we'll be examining a sample 
  of 26,559 stars in the Milky Way's halo with low metallicities, ranging from 
  -1.7 to -2.6, in the solar neighborhood using spectroscopic data. These data 
  were collected as part of the APOGEE-2 survey and cover a wide range of 
  stellar masses. We applied a machine learning-based approach to distinguish 
  stellar spectra from the Milky Way's background and removed the effects of 
  absorption resulting from the interaction between the Milky Way's gas and 
  halos. With this preprocessing complete, we were able to derive key 
  characteristics for each star, including its metallicity, a measure of 
  s-process element enrichment, and estimates of its mass and mass loss. 
  These characteristics reveal a sequence of galaxy evolution that includes 
  bulge-like, classical, and dwarf spheroidal phases, and shows that 
  extremely metal-poor stars in the Milky Way's halo tend to cluster around 
  open star clusters known as blue nucleated clusters that form through the 
  merger of low-mass dwarf galaxies. These findings also reveal a link 
  between the Milky Way's halo and the bulge-like phase of galaxy evolution, 
  and suggest that the classical dwarf spheroidal phase may be a transient 
  state. The paper concludes with a discussion of its results in the context 
  of the Milky Way's assembly through the merger of small galaxies.

In these realms, it's essential to understand how the model makes predictions and rely on its explanations. In response to these challenges, researchers have developed various techniques for interpreting neural networks, including saliery methods that identify sensitive features used for classification. However, these methods fail the test of robustness when input data is modified, as they produce inconsistent explanations for the same prediction. This issue is particularly pronounced when analyzing peer-data, as commonly seen in social media-based classification tasks. To address this problem, we propose an end-to-end framework called Explanation Steeper, which produces robust and data-explanations along with the predicted output. This framework incorporates an encoder for feature extraction and two separate decoders that generate class probabilities and explanations via saliery maps. To enforce the uniqueness of explanations and their robustness, we employ an auto-encoder structure and a minimax game-based challenge, respectively. As a result, our model delivers explanations that remain stable across different input data and can be confidently relied upon for decision-making. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline techniques in terms of explanation stability and reliability. The code for our proposed framework called Explanation Steeper is available at: https://github.com/yinghagosson/Explanation-Steeper.  We further introduce a new assessment metric called Reliability Explanaion Score (RES) to gauge the reliability of artificial neural network-based explanation techniques. Consequently, we propose an improved version of the RES metric, which is suitable for evaluating the reliability of artificial neural network-based explanation techniques in real-world scenarios. difficulties in resolving large-scale inverse problems lies in the requirement for regularizers to be informed about the underlying structure or patterns within the solution.  Despite significant interest in inverse problems with partially known components, research on problems with fully understood structure or patterns on a global scale faces significant obstacles.  These challenges stem from the need for regularizers to recognize the inherent patterns or underlying structure of the solution.  This report addresses the specific problem of a deconvolution task, where the underlying signal possesses a Fourier transform that exhibits significant magnitudes only within a limited frequency range.  An efficient strategy is presented to tackle this issue by utilizing the knowledge of the restricted support of the Fourier transform of the signal.  Specifically, the problem is re-cast as an inverse problem with positivity constraint and total variation regularization, where the goal is to recover the signal by minimizing the L2-norm of the residual, subject to constraints on the adjoint operator and the total variation of the solution.  Theoretical convergence rate estimates are established for a simplified version of the problem.  Numerical experiments are also presented to demonstrate the performance of the proposed method.  The problem is further generalized to include Gaussian damping.  An algorithm based on operator integration and fixed point iteration is proposed to solve the problem.  The convergence of the algorithm is theoretically analyzed, and its efficiency is demonstrated through numerical experiments.  The algorithm is implemented using the PETSc library for the finite element discretization.  The source code of the algorithm is made available online.  The algorithm is applied to a realistic deconvolution task involving a realistic operator.  The results show that the algorithm is an efficient tool for recovering signals from the continuous wavelet transform coefficients.  The code is available at https://github.com/Shu625/invproblem. Specifically, we analyze the eigenvalues of a matrix whose entries are defined by the weights of a quasi-permutation character under the irreducible representation of Sn. Here, we derive an important insight - the eigenvalues of this matrix are invariant under the action of a particular subgroup of S2n, which we term the minimal symmetry group. However, most existing applications of ZK-MACs require the verifier to be fully satisfied with the proof, which can be a limitation. In contrast, our research focuses on the more flexible case where the verifier can be partially satisfied with the proof, which we term as "relaxed" verification. We aim to achieve this through the efficient construction of a zero-knowledge protocol for proving knowledge of a particular private value $x$, given a public function $f$, while utilizing a MAC-based zero-knowledge proof system. Specifically, our construction, which we call "Relaxation Token" (RT), features a relaxed zero-knowledge proof whose "acceptance" probability is proportional to the corresponding "challenge" parameter $\gamma$, and is accompanied by a zero-knowledge protocol for which the verification process is either successful or results in the sender learning nothing about the private value $x$. Furthermore, our construction RT is based on a particular zero-knowledge proof system whose description can be omitted. Additionally, we demonstrate the versatility of RT by integrating it into various secure computation protocols. Thus, our research on RT serves as an exemplary model for secure computation protocols that are capable of withstanding some level of verification error. the early universe could have significant effects on cosmic evolution.  As a magnetic field interacts with plasma, it generates resistivity, which in turn affects rapid scalar field oscillations during inflation.  We examine the constraints on initial magnetic field strengths, specifically in relation to an invariant scale, as they impact residual scalar fluctuations and the resulting lensing signals.  Our analysis shows that strong magnetic fields, particularly those above $10^{-5}$ seconds, are unlikely due to the limitations of resistivity during inflation; however, faster inflationary roll-offs could significantly relax these constraints.  Additionally, we find that initial magnetic fields in the range of $10^{-12}$ to $10^{-9}$ seconds are potentially compatible with observational data from the cosmic microwave background, with a characteristic polarization signal that could be confirmed through future satellite missions.  We also consider post-inflationary magnetic field generation and show that strong resistivity during this period does not significantly impact the spectrum of curvature fluctuations.  Overall, our research emphasizes the importance of modeling resistivity during both inflationary and post-inflationary stages when studying the effects of magnetic fields on cosmic evolution.  We further highlight the potential for future studies to explore the effects of magnetic fields on the massive scalar field oscillations that drive the cosmic evolution, particularly in relation to the formation of primordial black holes.  The code used in this research is included as a supplementary material.  We also outline a modified version of the public Monte Carlo code \textsc{camb} to incorporate the effects of magnetic fields on cosmic evolution.  The results from this research are compatible with a wide range of magnetic field strengths, with an invariant scale ranging from $10^{-12}$ to $10^{-9}$ seconds, which could be explored in further studies using the modified \textsc{camb} code. about the uncertainty of future electricity demands, which is crucial for managing renewable energy sources and ensuring the stability of power grids. Despite the availability of reliable historical data for forecasting, the inherent randomness of current electricity consumption makes it difficult to model. To tackle this challenge, researchers have been examining the underlying stochastic processes of electricity consumption using theoretical models. Although these models have been successfully applied to modeling past consumption patterns, their effectiveness in capturing the true nature of future consumption has not been consistently demonstrated. This study leverages the empirical characteristics of random variables derived from the underlying processes and reveals that the sum of these variables converges to a Gaussian distribution with mean variance, which can be estimated from historical data. We then develop a load forecasting method based on this understanding. To accommodate the complexity of real-world consumption patterns, our approach incorporates a variety of statistical models to estimate the parameters of the Gaussian distribution. As a result, our method achieves accurate predictions of load forecasts and their corresponding uncertainties in multiple scenarios. Our empirical evaluation of grid-based and building-based load forecasts across various locations highlights the versatility and performance of this approach.   labeled data for supervised training poses a significant challenge for real-world
  applications of deep learning in unsupervised and semi-supervised scenarios.
  The abundance of unlabeled data in these scenarios could be leveraged to
  improve the accuracy of supervised learning models by using transfer learning.
  The process involves finding an optimal supervised learning model that
  minimizes the loss between the predicted and actual labels for a limited set
  of labeled data, while maximizing the similarity between the predicted labels
  and actual labels for a large set of unlabeled data.
  This paper refers to this combined problem as a supervised learning knowledge
  distillation problem, and proposes to solve it using reinforcement learning
  knowledge distillation, a process that involves training a supervisor using
  the sparse labeled data, and a learner using the abundant unlabeled data.
  The supervisor encourages the learner to focus on the most informative data
  samples by providing a soft label for each sample, in the form of a
  distribution over the possible labels, and rewards the learner for producing
  a sample whose predicted label matches the provided soft label.
  This paper presents theoretical evidence that the supervised learning knowledge
  distillation framework can transfer useful information from the abundant unlabeled
  data to the sparse labeled data, and empirical results showing its
  superiority to the traditional transfer learning methods using the abundant
  unlabeled data as a whole. The proposed method is useful for a wide range
  of supervised learning applications in the face of limited data, including
  semi-supervised learning, multi-domain learning, and weakly supervised
  learning. The code for the proposed method is publicly available at

often require rigorous data privacy protection to prevent sensitive information leaks.
  To address this challenge, the Differential Privacy framework provides theoretically supported privacy mechanisms to minimize the risk of individual data disclosure.
  In this research, we focus on developing an economically feasible algorithm to maintain privacy in databases containing the transaction records of multiple individuals.
  The goal of this database search algorithm aims to accurately identify all instances of a specified item within the database while adhering to $\delta$-differential privacy.
  To achieve this, we introduce a new mechanism based on binary search that can be leveraged multiple times to scan the database for a given target.
  Each search is designed to yield a privately accessible binary outcome ($\text{yes}$ or $\text{no}$) indicating the presence or absence of the target item in the specified range of the database.
  The algorithmic framework developed in this research can be used to train machine learning models and provides explicit solutions for commonly encountered problems such as finding the maximum value, calculating the sum, and identifying the most frequent item in the database.
  To demonstrate the versatility of this database search algorithm, we also explore its application in more complex machine learning models involving the aggregation of multiple databases.
  Throughout this research, we prioritize economically feasible solutions and focus on algorithms with low cost per search while maintaining optimal global differential privacy.
  In particular, we propose a nationally applicable pricing plan for this search algorithm based on the transaction records of a typical e-commerce platform.
  To further solidify the theoretical foundation of this research, we also provide formally proven guarantees on the accuracy of the machine learning models trained using this search algorithm.
  Additionally, we compare our proposed solution with alternative economically feasible algorithms and demonstrate the existence of vast, untapped economic opportunities resulting from the scalable nature of this database search algorithm.
  To facilitate the implementation of this research in real-world scenarios, we have open-sourced our code and made our formally proven theoretical results publicly available.  In the process, we have also established an innovative application of this database search algorithm in deep learning, which has yielded a globally differential privacy compatible neural network capable of achieving precision comparable to non-private models.  To further advance the development of economically feasible differentially private machine learning solutions, we propose an open research agenda that emphasizes the integration of complex machine learning models with large-scale transaction databases.  As evidence of the practical utility of this research, we have implemented a nationally applicable pricing plan for the search algorithm and have already generated substantial economic returns for our institution.   widely utilized, allowing programs to cross the boundary between single and
  multiple-task functionality. Initially, researchers focused on analyzing single
  neural network behavior but have given little thought to the underlying principles
  of multi-task neural networks. In response, we've conducted an in-depth study of
  linear multi-task neural networks, unveiling the underlying structure and
  mechanistic explanations for their behavior. Surprisingly, we've found that these
  networks can be reduced to multiple independent single-task networks that share
  inputs but have distinct outputs, thereby capturing the essence of multi-tasking.
  Through our theoretical findings, we've also identified key factors that influence
  the ability of these networks to generalize across multiple tasks, including the
  size of the hidden layer. In addition, we've developed a framework that enables
  us to analyze and compare the underlying representations learned for each task.

  single task does not necessarily result in the desired multi-tasking capabilities.

relational algebra presents significant challenges, primarily stemming from the lack of structural information about the algebra's inputs. However, for certain types of inputs, we can determine complex aspects of functions's properties. This research focuses on identifying the complexity of transitive closure functions in relation to inputs with finite ranks, and we demonstrate that for inputs with a rank of two, the transitive closure function's complexity is analogous to polynomial time, whereas for inputs with unlimited ranks, we establish that the transitive closure function's complexity is equivalent to linear exponential time. Moreover, we establish lower bounds on the complexity of transitive closure functions for inputs with varying ranks, revealing that the complexity is sensitive to the rank and decreases as the rank increases. Furthermore, we show that our findings converge with existing results when considering inputs without any structural constraints. Additionally, we discuss implications of our findings on the complexity of evaluating transitive closure functions for specific types of infinite inputs. This text also introduces new criteria for comparing the speeds at which functions compute over infinite inputs, and we hope it serves as a starting point for an in-depth investigation of this aspect. This research is an extension of my previous work on the complexity of transitive closure functions for inputs with finite ranks. However, this expanded text now includes a newly established result on the complexity of finite unravelling functions, as well as a result on the closure of R.E. sets under finite unravelling, which can be obtained using a recently discovered connection between unravelling functions and partial order reductions. Moreover, our findings are supported by new lower bounds on the complexity of transitive closure functions for inputs with varying ranks. F) experiment on the Russian Sector of the International Space Station has been operational since 2011, allowing for the study of plasma properties in low Earth orbit. With a dedicated power and data transmission system, the FPF device measures fluctuations in the floating potential of a spacecraft-mounted metal surface to obtain information about local plasma conditions. The straightforward yet effective approach has yielded significant insights into plasma behavior, particularly in the region between 30 and 60 kilometers above sea level, and has also monitored space weather events impacting the spacecraft. The robust design of the FPF setup has minimized interference from electronic components and spacecraft systems, yielding results that are highly relevant to the development of future spacecraft. The experiment has continuously collected data ever since its deployment and has already provided valuable information about a critical layer of the Earth's atmosphere. The durability of the device has exceeded expectations and it is expected to operate for the remainder of the space station's mission. The successful data collected by the FPF experiment has also prompted interest in similar measurements on future spacecraft. The code developed for processing FPF data has been made publicly available on the website of the Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology. The code is written in MATLAB and IDL and includes both the initial data processing and the interpretation of those results in the context of local plasma conditions. The code also includes an option for processing data from the DCCT device, which is used to calibrate the ion flux measurements obtained from the RPC device. The code is available for download at [https://www.physu.ru/en/science/research/fpf/code/](https://www.physu.ru/en/science/research/fpf/code/). The complete dataset from the FPF experiment can be obtained from the NASA Space Data System under the project code RPX1. The same code is also used for processing data from the similar RAPLOF device, which is part of the Tianwen-1 Mars Orbiter launched in July 2020. The code developed for processing FPF data has also been used for processing data from the similar FLPT device, which is part of the Mars Global Remote Sensing Experiment Package launched on the Mars 2020 rover in July 2020. The code is being used for processing data from the similar instruments on the Mars Sample Return orbiters to be launched in the mid 2020s.   images encountered in real-world scenarios differ substantially from those used

Specifically, we consider the system's dynamics in a semiclassical setting where the photon field is divided into a classical component and a quantum part. Our analysis shows that the particle's Hamiltonian possesses a magnetic translation symmetry, and we identify the classical component of the photon field as a magnetic force and a dielectric constant that result from the averaging process. Accurate determination of this component, known as the $E$-mode, is crucial as it can provide information about the source of gravitational waves. We examine the prospects of detecting the $E$-mode in the specific case of a binary black hole merger event. Gravitational waves' polarization components interact with an object's spin, resulting in a signal that can either add to the $E$-mode (synchronous signal) or subtract from it (asynchronous signal). The LISA detector's response, influenced by its long baseline and rotating configuration, can be modeled using a combination of harmonic analysis. This approach enables the identification of the $E$-mode (referred to as the "plane perpendicular component") in the accelerometer data. The strength of the signal in the detector frame is expressed as a fraction of the signal strength in the free field, and is found to range from 0.003 for the asynchronous component to 0.64 for the synchronous component. The likelihood of detecting the $E$-mode in a signal duration of one year from a billion binary black hole merger events is then calculated. Assuming a signal-to-noise ratio of eight for detection, the probability of doing so is found to be 0.11, or 11%. This percentage indicates that, on average, one out of every nine such events will yield a measurable $E$-mode signal. This probability decreases to 0.03, or 3%, for events with an initial mass ratio of three or more. The likelihood of detecting the $E$-mode in specific mass bins is also examined. The signal-to-noise ratio required for detection can be reduced to two by either increasing the signal duration to two years, or by employing a detector with a ten times lower acceleration noise. Specifically, we found that ACLR leads to larger networks with a greater dynamic range of the memory cell, resulting in a more than twofold increase in network size without a corresponding increase in training errors. high-performance computing systems. As a significant consumer of energy, the memory hierarchy of modern computers presents a substantial barrier to efficient and scalable technology. Interconnect-based memory systems can mitigate this challenge by dynamically reconfiguring memory interconnects to minimize energy expenditure while maintaining high performance. A new model of a wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM) memory interconnect is introduced here, featuring a high-speed spatial interconnect with multiple data paths and a traffic-aware frequency allocator. This unique model allows for optimal frequency allocation in the memory hierarchy to maximize energy efficiency and system performance. A specialized instruction set and optimized compiler directives are also presented to facilitate seamless WDM memory access from application-level code. Extensive simulations of real-world applications on real hardware demonstrate significant improvements in energy efficiency and system performance when using the WDM memory interconnect, with results showing up to 5.5 times lower energy consumption and 3 times better overall system performance compared to state-of-the-art memory systems. To further demonstrate the scalability and efficiency of this model, a working prototype of the WDM memory system was built using an FPGA, with results showing an order of magnitude decrease in energy consumption when using the WDM memory interconnect. To facilitate widespread adoption, the WDM memory interconnect is being made available as an open-source toolchain, with the goal of easily integrating this technology into future memory hierarchy designs. The research presented here provides a foundation for the design of future memory hierarchies that can efficiently support high-performance computing systems while meeting growing energy efficiency demands. the brain's default mode network (DMN) has yet to be fully discovered. Our current knowledge is mainly based on static imaging analyses, which fail to capture the dynamic characteristics of the system. Recent advances in neurophysiological recordings with high temporal and spatial resolution hope to reveal the missing aspects of the DMN. Specifically, investigations using functional connectome dynamics have uncovered a state of elevated connectivity within the DMN during task-free periods. We propose an analytical approach that leverages dimensionality reduction and state-space models to study the spatial and temporal dimensions of brain connectivity. Our method allows for the identification of distinct connectivity states across different cognitive tasks. Notably, our findings with human subjects reveal a complex network architecture in the DMN, characterized by a set of linear regulators that govern the system's dynamics and ensure the persistence of a particular, highly connected state during task-free periods. In contrast, the system responds differently to various types of tasks, exhibiting a lack of persistence and instead displaying a tendency to shift to a network configuration that is optimized for task-specific information processing. Our research provides a quantitative framework for understanding the nonlinear, three-dimensional dynamics of the DMN, and our results offer a glimpse into the precise mechanisms governing the system's temporal, spatial, and cognitive aspects. Ultimately, our findings highlight the importance of a state-space approach in uncovering the fundamental properties of the DMN. To facilitate further research, we have made our analytical method, along with the IFC model and the Baysian estimation tools used in this study, openly accessible through an accompanying code repository. As demonstrated by our results, this approach also holds significant implications for developing a biological generalization of the MDP framework that can be utilized in cutting-edge artificial intelligence applications. computational model originally developed 
  for simulating primate visual cortex function, specifically the perception 
  of form and motion. Initially created using MATLAB, UDIVA features a 
  detailed neural network with 121 nodes, each representing a distinct brain 
  component, and is notable for its integration of form and motion processing 
  pathways. The model incorporates three primary components based on 
  neurobiological evidence: 
  1. Local neural processing, where simple cells process visual inputs in 
     different spatial frequencies.
  2. Horizontal neural connections, which mimic the behavior of complex cells 
     through their suppression of local grid patterns.
  3. Vertical neural connections, representing the projection of complex cells 
     onto higher-order cells and the resulting generation of motion percepts.
  To evaluate UDIVA, three experiments were conducted: 
  Experiment 1 tested the model's ability to detect forms of varying 
  complexity and found that its sensitivity to these forms, as indicated by 
  gamma-band activity, correlates with the mathematical concept of 
  fourier energy. Experiment 2 examined the model's motion perception and 
  discovered that its ability to detect motion, as represented by beta-band 
  activity, optimally processes frequencies associated with bradylocomotion.
  Experiment 3 assessed the model's ability to prioritize form over motion 
  perception and found that this capability is reflected in the shift from 
  gamma-band to beta-band activity as motion frequencies increase.
  These findings demonstrate that UDIVA accurately replicates primate visual 
  cortex function and, through its neural network, provides insights into the 
  computational processes underlying form and motion perception. The model 
  also offers a promising basis for the neural treatment of visual disorders 
  affecting form and motion perception, such as those experienced in 
  amblyopia. The MATLAB code for UDIVA is freely available at the MATLAB 
  File Exchange, and future developments of the model will be made through 
  this platform. The current version of the code can be obtained using 
  search term "UDIVA" at the MATLAB website. 
  This research was supported by grants from the National Science Foundation 
  and the National Institutes of Health. 
  In addition to its scientific value, UDIVA has practical applications in 
  the treatment of amblyopia, a visual disorder affecting form and motion 
  perception, and a case study is presented here. The study involves a 
  9-year-old amblyopic patient

Currently available state-of-the-art models fail to handle graphs with a billion edges due to their high memory usage and computing power requirements. This research paper introduces an over-smoothing prevention technique called graph patchNetwork (GPN), which incorporates a novel feature extraction approach called patch-based representation learning.   native Finnish speakers, a notable contrast emerged between the most
  frequent and the least frequent responses to a particular word.
  The most common associations fell into three categories: synonyms,
  related concepts, and antonyms. In contrast, the least frequent
  responses consisted mainly of opposite extremes, exemplified by
  associations like "day--night," "life--death," or "good--evil."
  These extreme opposites are infrequently linked to each other in
  everyday language, making them more likely to be remembered from
  word associations tasks. Furthermore, research has shown that such
  opposites are readily recalled due to their emotional intensity and
  heightened cognitive accessibility. Consequently, the frequency of
  word associations can serve as an indirect indicator of a word's
  opposites within the Finnish language. 
  The research also involved analyzing a large corpus of written Finnish
  text, specifically the opposites that arise from the use of certain
  grammatical structures, such as superlatives ("the biggest") or
  negations ("not happy"). While these constructed opposites are
  relevant to the language, they are not as inherently contrasting as
  the word associations provided by native speakers. 
  The study focuses primarily on the emotional and cognitive aspects
  of opposites in the Finnish language and less on the structural or
  semantic aspects. It reveals significant variability among the least
  frequent word associations, suggesting that each pair of opposites
  must be examined individually rather than being lumped together. 
  The most intense opposites, such as life and death, stand out as
  the most cognitively accessible and frequently remembered within
  the Finnish language. 
  The methodology section explains how a list of 60 opposite pairs
  was derived from the results of the word associations study conducted

  of word associations among native speakers of the Finnish language. 
  It suggests that the distinctive characteristics of the Finnish language

  which native speakers recall the opposites within that language.

in animation, a computationally demanding task that involves replicating the movement of a source character onto a target character with a distinct body structure. Our character deformation toolkit utilizes a intermediate character as a reference to maintain physical consistency between the source, intermediate, and target characters. If the intermediate and target characters are fully detailed 3D models, we achieve the desired results using their shared mesh data. If the target character's model is incomplete, we employ a level-of-detail technique based on mesh decomposition. By selecting a suitable subset of the target character's features to mimic, we optimize the fit of the source character's movement to the remaining, non-mimicked features. Our approach significantly reduces the computational demands of human deformation transfer. We further extend our method to accommodate characters represented by statistical models, such as those generated by avatars and EMAs, by reconstructing the target character's 3D model from which the statistical model was derived.   multilateration is a common technique in device localization. However, by
  introducing movement into the scenario, estimating the 3D position of a device
  becomes far more complex and requires the analysis of data from multiple
  sensors. In an attempt to simplify this process, our research assumes that

  significant computational power and memory for the sensor, which could be an

  enhanced our understanding of red giant stars. Specifically, they have enabled 
  us to investigate subgiants with a precision that was previously unattainable, 
  and to analyze their rotational influences on elemental synthesis through mass 
  transfer in binary systems. The {\it Gaia} satellite has provided accurate 
  distances for a substantial number of red giant stars, allowing for the detection

  rotational splitting in oscillation modes in the spectrum of a subgiant rotating 
  slowly enough for differential rotation to become apparent. This landmark finding 
  confirms the presence of differential rotation in red giant stars and offers a 
  direct link to mass transfer in binary systems. However, it also indicates that 
  binary merger products and extremely fast rotators may exhibit a different oscillatory 
  signature than previously assumed. As a consequence, we are now facing a more 
  complex picture of chemical enrichment through mass transfer in binary systems, 
  and a larger percentage of subgiants with companions will need to be accounted 
  for in models of chemical enrichment. Furthermore, we need to reevaluate our 
  understanding of the rotational mixing process in red giant stars, and a 
  distinction needs to be made between the behavior of single stars and those 
  with mass transfer in their past. This newfound understanding also positions 
  red giant stars rotating sufficiently to exhibit differential rotation as critical 
  objects for solving the long-standing problem of chemical enrichment through mass 
  transfer in binary systems.

In this setting, the Koopman operator can be defined as a composition of operators, each associated with a specific region. This connection facilitates the utilization of operator spectral theory to investigate the ergodicity of the system. The validity of this approach is demonstrated through the simulation of multiple system examples with both continuous and discrete components. The simulated data confirms the accuracy of the method, while the computation time is found to be significantly reduced when utilizing a compositional representation of the Koopman operator. The new program can perform both forward and reverse mode automatic differentiation, supporting common mathematical operations including functions like sine and exponential, as well as more complex functions derived from these basic functions. However, the limitation of source-to-source transformation leads to a restricted input format for the original program, thus requiring a significant amount of preprocessing. To mitigate this limitation, we created a version of the software that uses the Java Standard Library for mathematical operations, resulting in a more flexible input format at the cost of longer computation times due to object creation and method invocation. As a result, the original and modified versions of the software exhibit distinct input and output formats of the pre- and postprocessing stages, making it necessary to reapply the transformation to achieve the original output. Nevertheless, the modified version outperforms the original one in terms of computation time for the automatic differentiation of large programs, by a factor of up to 4.5 times. Furthermore, our experiments reveal that using method invocation instead of direct function calls when performing mathematical operations on scalars leads to a doubling of the computation time, while using arrays or vectors as input leads to a significant increase of up to 7 times in computation time due to memory allocation and management. To address this issue, we propose optimizing the design of automatic differentiation tools by combining source-to-source transformation with embedded runtime environment functionality, and support for object-oriented programming to minimize overhead costs. As proof of concept, we reconfigured the Java Standard Library to provide a runtime environment that supports reverse mode automatic differentiation with adjoint objects, resulting in a significant improvement of computation time by factors of 6.5 to 43.5 times depending on the specific operations performed. details associated with 1184 spectroscopic observations of 773 stars gathered during 12 years of observations with the High Accuracy Radial velocity Telescope (HARPS). The observations were conducted at the La Silla Observatory and encompass a time frame from 1998 to 2011. The data comprise radial velocity measurements along with various atmospheric and temperature readings for each star. The data analysis involves combining the light collected from spectral companions to derive the properties of primary stars in binary systems. The resulting dataset includes measurements of radial velocity, spectral type, metallicity, temperature, and luminosity for 773 stars. The data show that 206 of these stars have been identified as potential planetary host stars. The dataset also includes 345 giant stars that could host planets and 64 supergiant stars with little information on their planetary systems. The complete dataset, along with reduced data for individual stars, is available through the HEAnet repository. The data release is marked by a citation of the paper listed under doi: 10.5201/aas.2018.9349. This work develops a non-parametric method to estimate the unobserved states and account for information-based state dependence, effectively capturing the sequential interdependence of treatments.   This study introduces a novel class of ANNs known as Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), which outperforms traditional artificial neural networks in various aspects such as calculation efficiency, memory consumption, and power usage. As a result, our model exhibits remarkable performance improvements in terms of energy efficiency, with a 32-fold enhancement in performance per unit energy consumption.

  techniques have already shown significant potential in identifying particles such

  by the rapid progress achieved in computer vision and language processing tasks.

  challenging techniques like meta-learning, neural memory, and neural field theories.  
  We also outline a proposed roadmap for future research, highlighting key problems  
  in particle physics that could be addressed using these sophisticated techniques.  
  By presenting code examples and outlining experimental setups, we strive to make  
  these complex concepts more accessible to researchers new to deep learning.  
  Ultimately, we hope this review and future studies on neural network applications  
  in particle physics will encourage collaboration and breakthroughs among physicists  
  and machine learning experts.  We also provide an online platform for code and  
  experimental results to facilitate replication and further development.

This research builds on previous findings from a similar study conducted in 2019. Given the age of these stars, the discovered planets are likely massive enough to influence the stars' masses and radii, which in turn could impact their mass and radius measurements obtained through transits and radial velocity methods. By calculating mass and radius measurements under the assumption of stable mass transfer, we found that the three new planets have masses between 80-100 times that of Jupiter and radii between 10-11 times that of Jupiter, significantly larger than Jupiter's radius. Notably, the most notable feature of these planets is their extremely thick atmospheres, which we predict will be confirmed through future observations with the James Webb Space Telescope. Additionally, we believe that extreme sub-Neptunes with similar properties may have formed around these stars and could be detected through high-cadence photometry. If so, these planets would be classified as the most significant variables among T Tauri associations and could potentially be identified through future observations. Based on their orbits, we speculate that these planets may have influenced the stars' binary or planetary migration processes. In the future, we recommend monitoring these planets with a combination of telescopes including the James Webb Space Telescope to gain a deeper understanding of their composition, as well as through high-cadence photometry to detect any internal heat-driven planetary expansion. Based on their sizes, these planets are unlikely to be retained by their stars in the long term and could be classified as the precursors to red giant stars. With further observations, we hope to gain a deeper understanding of these giant sub-Jovian planets and their potential for influencing their stars and surrounding environments.   systems with a continuous spectrum. Our theoretical findings also provide a

  the early detection of hypoxemia.  Conventional methods rely on bulk measurement
  techniques that have significant disadvantages, including slow measurement rates and
  limited spatial resolution in pulse oximetry.  To address these limitations, a
  compact, non-invasive oxygen saturation sensor based on frequency domain optical
  scanning tomography has been developed.  The sensor features a miniature reflectance
  type oximetry probe with an optical fiber flat-surface reflectance configuration.
  It measures reflected intensity at three different optical intensity depths and
  calculates oxygen saturation levels through empirical formulae.  The sensor was
  successfully tested on real-time breathing simulations and human subjects during
  normal and heavy breathing exercises.  In the experiment with the simulated lung
  model, the desaturation rates were 0.65 s and 1.13 s for slow and heavy breathing,
  respectively.  In the human subject experiment, the desaturation rates were 1.17
  s and 0.85 s for slow and heavy breathing, respectively.  The sensor demonstrated
  accurate oxygen saturation measurements across different breathing frequencies. 
  Further improvements are anticipated through the modification of the oximetry
  calculation algorithm and the use of a more accurate oximetry calculation method
  based on the measured optical signals.  The compact sensor offers significant
  performance enhancements over conventional methods and shows great potential for
  widespread hypoxemia detection applications. \\

  We examine the impact of these multi-field Q-balls on the universe through 
  numerical simulations and an energy density perturbation approach in a 
  semi-classical context. The outcome of these simulations can be broadly 
  categorized into three distinct scenarios: (1) if the multi-field Q-balls 
  primarily consist of a dominant field surrounded by a trivial phase of the 
  other field, then their annihilation process remains similar to that of a 
  single-field Q-ball; (2) when there is a significant phase of the dominant 
  field and a non-trivial phase of the sub-dominant field, a multi-bounce 
  oscillation pattern emerges that can lead to the creation of an endless 
  amount of Q-ball matter; (3) in cases where all complex scalar fields have 
  a non-trivial phase, especially if they have a similar energy density, 
  their annihilation can result in an explosive outcome.
  Our semi-classical approach also reveals that the total energy of multi-field 
  Q-balls can significantly differ from that of single-field Q-balls, with 
  values ranging from a minimal amount to an exponentially large amount, 
  indicating that the annihilation process of multi-field Q-balls is highly 
  unpredictable and needs to be evaluated on a case-by-case basis. 
  Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the entropy of multi-field Q-balls 
  is an unstable parameter that can suddenly increase exponentially during 
  oscillations. 
  Our research implies that the formation of multi-field Q-balls within the 
  early universe could act as a feasible mechanism to generate the vast 
  amount of matter necessary for the universe's current state. 
  However, it is crucial to consider the consequences of multi-field Q-balls 
  on the universe's evolution through more comprehensive simulations that 
  take into account quantum effects and the influence of the surrounding 
  perturbed metric. 
  It is also noteworthy to mention that the semi-classical approach used 
  in this study has previously been applied to the study of multi-field 
  cosmological perturbations in a quadratic potential scenario. 
  It is also important to note that the term "non-trivial phase" in this 
  study refers to a phase where the energy density of the sub-dominant field 
  is comparable to that of the dominant field.

  is highly versatile and suitable for a range of problems, including

  forecasting tasks. The VGG-style DRRNN, a module-specific implementation

Real-world crowd anomaly detection challenges are addressed by a multi-stage framework consisting of novel Deep Trimmed Frequency-Specific Sparse Regression (DFSSR) and crowd anomaly instance flagging Deep Trimmed Frequency-Specific Discriminator (DFSD).  The proposed approach begins with DFSSR, which employs deep feature extractors to obtain anomaly frequency-specific sparse codes, from which the threshold for anomaly detection is derived. We utilize this theory to examine the stochastic thermodynamics of a nonequilibrium steady state achieved in a driven Bose-Joseimhima quench dynamics system.  Our findings show that the system's nonequilibrium steady-state state can be fully characterized by its work distribution, which is determined by the system's equilibrium properties in the quench regime. As a result, we are able to demonstrate that the system's nonequilibrium steady-state state exhibits a temperature asymmetry that is directly related to a second-order phase transition that occurs in the quench regime, and we believe that this finding represents a fundamental example of a nonequilibrium steady-state system that is driven by quenches.  We also anticipate that the system's nonequilibrium steady-state state's temperature asymmetry, as well as the associated entropy production asymmetry, could be investigated through theoretical or numerical methods involving multiple quench regimes or driven Bose-Joseimhima systems. This phenomenon was first observed by Lerch and later studied by Berry, Condon, and others. In 1936, Riemann initially expressed the Zeta function in terms of the Gamma function, resulting in functions exhibiting Stokes layers. However, it was not until 2004 that the deepest origin of the Stokes phenomenon was identified within the Riemann Zeta function itself. This research aims to extend the (extended) Beta and Gamma functions, initially defined for positive real numbers, to the complex plane, and to illustrate the Stokes phenomenon through the analytic continuation of these functions. Specifically, we will show that the extended Beta function can be expressed in terms of the Riemann Zeta function and exhibit the Stokes layers of this connection. Moreover, we will derive the residues at the poles of the extended Gamma function to exhibit the relationship between these poles and the zeros or poles of the Riemann Zeta function, thereby providing the key to understanding the Stokes layers. Furthermore, we will introduce an iterative process that retrieves the original series expansion of the extended Beta function, and to that end, we will modify the process to obtain the extended Gamma function from its exponential integral representation. Additionally, we will utilize our results to describe the location of the zeros of the Riemann Zeta function in the critical plane and to derive the values of the zeros in the upper half-plane through the extended Beta function. Finally, we will discuss the connection between the zeros of the Riemann Zeta function and the Gaussian distribution and to that end, we will introduce a new statistical model that generates random zeros of the Riemann Zeta function. This research builds upon the work of Edinburgh and Accioly, Gelfand, and Kilburn, and incorporates results on the residues at the poles of the extended Gamma function from the research of Edinburgh and Accioly, Gelfand, and Kilburn in combination with the values of the zeros in the upper half-plane derived by Condon, Sarnak, and Rudnick and the Conjecture of the distribution of the zeros of the Riemann Zeta function in the critical plane initially proposed by Hardy and Ramanujan. Previous studies have demonstrated the presence of name-to-appearance and appearance-to-name correspondences in deep neural network feature spaces.  To take advantage of these correspondences for object classification, this paper proposes a new method, based on a contrastive learning technique, to transfer knowledge from the name-to-appearance correspondences.  The proposed framework consists of an encoding module for object representation and a contrastive learning module for knowledge transfer.  Object encoding is achieved using a generalized Swish network and ReLU in a two-branch structure.  The contrastive learning module employs a semantic map, feature map, and triplet loss to learn the desired object classifier.  Experimental evaluations on four real-world object classification datasets show that the proposed method surpasses regularized contrastive learning in an unconditional setting and state-of-the-art methods in an unconditional and conditional setting.  The proposed approach is efficient and effective, as evidenced by our model's minimal parameters and the presence of name-to-appearance correspondences in its feature space.  To further validate the proposed hypothesis, we remove the name-to-appearance correspondences by fine-tuning the model and observe a performance decline.  The proposed method's general applicability is demonstrated by using pre-trained models on the LLaMA dataset for natural language processing tasks like sentiment analysis and text classification.  The proposed approach is suitable for real-world deployment due to its lightweight nature, as shown by our dataset downgrade test.  The proposed model's fairness is assessed by evaluating its classification based on the ML Fairness Framework, and our results indicate a significant improvement in the $F_{\phi}$-score.  The proposed code is available at https://github.com/zhengayecg/CName2A.  The proposed approach has implications for both the computer vision and natural language processing communities, as it provides a universally applicable way to enhance the quality of models without requiring problem-specific knowledge.  To encourage progress in this direction, we propose a new research question: What features of the corresponding relations are extractable and valuable for the corresponding objects?  To address this question, we propose a new benchmark, CName2A-Bench, which is a set of corresponding relations with both the corresponding objects' names and appearances available, and a new evaluation metric, CCorr-F1, which is a fusion of the corresponding objects' names and appearances.  The proposed CName2A model achieves an CCorr-F1 score of 0.83

assembly problem asks for the maximum number of monomer units that can be successfully placed in a plane through tile-based assembly, assuming a particular set of tiles is available. This problem has different variants, including one where tile placement is allowed without regard to orientation. In the case where tile placement is allowed both horizontally and vertically, the assembly model known as RNA folding model offers an interesting variant. Here we examine the RNA folding model variant where assembly is done without regard to orientation and present two main contributions. Firstly, we establish a tight bound of ($5\times 2^k$) on the maximum size of a plane of size $5\times 5$ that can be achieved through k-monomer assembly, and also outline a strategy to assemble planes of any size up to $k$. Secondly, we provide an explicit formula for calculating the maximum size of a plane of a given height without regard to orientation and show that this formula leads to an efficient algorithm for checking validity of a given plane assembly configuration in O(k) time. Additionally, we demonstrate an innovative approach to enhance the plane size by introducing "dummy" monomers, leading to a more efficient use of space. Lastly, we conclude our discussion by reviewing related works and proposing several open problems on the planar assembly problem.   high-level image processing applications.  Multi-view stereo reconstruction
  algorithms aim to replace missing pixel intensity values in images with accurately
  interpolated values, based on neighboring views.  Real-world images pose a
  significant challenge to dense image matching algorithms due to their intricate
  detail, varying texture, and extensive amount of image data.  To tackle this
  issue, researchers have developed a wide variety of methods in recent years.
  Evaluating the performance of dense image matching algorithms on real-world
  images involves two primary challenges: designing a comprehensive real-world
  image dataset and developing an unbiased metrics to assess their performance.
  To address the first challenge, we assembled an extensive real-world image
  dataset called DOOMed, comprising an unprecedented 30 gigapixels of free-form
  natural scenery without any restrictions on image capture methods.
  To address the second challenge, we crafted an innovative two-staged metrics
  to evaluate performance based on both 3D reconstruction accuracy and algorithm
  robustness to varying input images.
  Our proposed metrics demonstrate a striking disparity between state-of-the-art
  algorithm performance on controlled versus real-world images, highlighting
  the limitations of current multi-view stereo reconstruction algorithms when
  confronted with free-form natural scenery. 
  Our research delivers three primary contributions: a vast, no-cost real-world
  image dataset called DOOMed of an unprecedented scale in gigapixels, a detailed
  guide on constructing such a dataset, and a set of comprehensive metrics to
  evaluate the performance of multi-view stereo reconstruction algorithms on real-world
  images with an emphasis on their robustness to varying input images. 
  Our research also leads to the creation of a new, publicly available benchmark
  called Doom Challenge to advance the development of real-world natural scenery
  density estimation algorithms.

A recent study optimizes the use of a deep learning tool, known as a neural network, to pinpoint the characteristics of a multi-body decay process that involves an unknown initial particle.  Specifically, it was assumed that a direct detection experiment revealed a scattering event between an ordinary matter particle and an unknown initial particle that resulted in two observable particles.  By training a neural network on a large set of multi-body decay simulations, it was possible to predict the two-body final state for a typical direct detection scenario.  As a result, researchers were able to identify the characteristics of an unknown initial particle from a multi-body decay process.  Furthermore, it was demonstrated that this approach is effective even when the process is similar to those produced by the Standard Model of particle physics.  A similar analysis using traditional methods failed to accurately determine the two-body final state.  Consequently, this study confirms the utility of a neural network in identifying the characteristics of dark matter or other exotic matter through multi-body decay processes. high-energy nucleus-nucleus collisions is influenced by the quantum chromodynamics medium created in these collisions. As a result, the shape of this spectrum serves as a crucial indicator of the properties of this medium. In a new approach, we use leading neutron lepton pairs to investigate the structure of the spectrum in proton-proton and lead-lead collisions at the LHC. A specialized algorithm is employed to identify leading neutrons with a large longitudinal momentum gap, and subsequently, lepton pairs are matched to these neutrons. A thorough study of various kinematic variables reveals that the spectrum of leading lepton pairs is largely unaffected by the collision system and shows a similar pattern to radiative processes. Furthermore, a theoretical model predicting the production of leading neutrons in proton-proton collisions is used to simulate the production of leading lepton pairs. A comparison between theoretical predictions and experimental data shows that the spectrum of leading lepton pairs can be explained by pure semi-leptonic processes and does not necessitate the involvement of the quantum chromodynamics medium. In conclusion, while the collision of two very fast moving nuclei can produce a large amount of long-range correlations in the spectrum of lepton pairs, a more comprehensive understanding of the structure of these correlations is needed to accurately extract information about the properties of the medium created in these collisions. (Mageac) experiment is an
  extensive air shower array that has been operational in India since 2017.
  With a large geographical coverage of over 3600 meters above sea level
  and a high-altitude laboratory in Goans Western Ghats, Mageac has a key

  This paper presents the detailed approach of Mageac's energy calculation
  method, focusing on the implementation of a simulated Monte Carlo system

  shower characteristics such as the maximum depth of the shower maximum,
  electromagnetic and muon component densities, and the energy of the air
